notes.meaning: God invites anyone who is spiritually thirsty to come and receive living water, wine, and milk. These drinks represent the deep blessings of the gospel, such as inner life, strength, and joy. Because Christ has already paid the full price through His own sacrifice, these gifts are offered completely free of charge to all who admit their need.

The Lord gently challenges people for pouring their money and energy into worldly things that cannot satisfy the soul. Earthly pleasures and human achievements are like food that leaves a person starving. True contentment comes only by listening to God and receiving the rich spiritual food He freely offers.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older critical scholars understood the bread, wine, and milk as literal material food and physical abundance awaiting the Jewish exiles when they returned home, rather than spiritual blessings.

notes.meaning: God calls everyone to bend their ear and come to Him so their souls may truly live. He promises to make an everlasting covenant—a binding, permanent agreement of friendship—with those who come. This agreement secures the same faithful, unfailing mercies promised to David, which find their fulfillment in the Messiah.

differ.view: Particular Baptists emphasize that people must be given spiritual life by God before they are able to hear and come to Christ in faith.
Methodists teach that the offer of the covenant is open to everyone, and any person who chooses to listen and respond can receive this gift of life.

notes.meaning: God appointed this royal figure to be a witness of divine truth to the surrounding nations, as well as their ruler and guide. While King David partially fulfilled this role, the promise points forward to Jesus Christ. As a faithful leader, He reveals God's will and guides His people in how to live.

differ.view: Some hold that this refers literally to the resurrected King David, who will reign as an earthly prince over Israel during a future thousand-year kingdom.

notes.meaning: The Messiah and His people will call out to distant Gentile nations that were once strangers to God's promises. Because the Lord has glorified His servant through great acts such as the resurrection, these foreign peoples will eagerly run to join Him. God's salvation expands far beyond Israel to embrace the entire world.

People are urged to seek the Lord and pray to Him while this favorable time of grace lasts. Right now God makes Himself close and ready to receive sinners. A day will eventually come, at death or final judgment, when that open door shuts and He can no longer be found.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the Hebrew grammar carries the sense of seeking the Lord while He actively makes Himself available or allows Himself to be approached.

notes.meaning: True repentance means abandoning bad actions and changing sinful thoughts and attitudes. When an unrighteous person turns back to God, the Lord does not hold a grudge. Instead, He meets them with tender compassion and freely forgives all their offenses.

differ.view: Some Calvinist Baptists emphasize that the thoughts to be abandoned include relying on one's own good deeds rather than being justified, or made right with God, by faith alone.
Methodists stress that returning to God must include sincere repentance that promptly produces an obedient and reformed daily life.

notes.meaning: God reminds His people that His way of thinking and acting is entirely different from theirs. Human beings are often stingy with mercy and quick to hold resentments when they are hurt. By contrast, the Lord is astonishingly eager to pardon anyone who sincerely repents.

Just as the sky sits vastly higher than the dirt of the earth, God's love and wisdom reach far beyond human understanding. People often struggle to believe God could forgive sins as terrible as theirs. This vast distance shows that His capacity to show mercy goes far beyond human limits.

Rain and snow fall from the sky and do not vanish into the air before they soak into the soil. They cause seeds to sprout, bringing forth grain for food right now and seeds to plant for the coming year. God uses the dependable cycles of the weather to illustrate how reliably His plans operate.

In the exact same way as the rain, the message that comes from God's mouth never returns to Him empty or unsuccessful. It works like an active messenger carrying out His perfect will. Every promise He gives, especially the promise to redeem His people, is certain to happen.

differ.view: Reformed commentators note that while God's word is entirely powerful, individuals can cut themselves off from enjoying its comforting fruit through their own stubborn unbelief.
Methodists read this verse specifically as an absolute guarantee that God's spoken promises to pardon even the greatest sinners will never fail.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular modern reading uses this verse to claim that quoting or praying Bible verses will always bring about the believer's personal desires, rather than recognizing that the verse promises God's own will to be fulfilled.

notes.meaning: God's people are promised a joyful departure and a peaceful journey home from their captivity. The scenery around them is poetically described as sharing in their gladness, with mountains bursting into song and trees clapping their branches. This joyful return also foreshadows the deep peace and relief that come with spiritual salvation.

Instead of painful thorns and briers, noble cypress and sweet-smelling myrtle trees will flourish. This dramatic change points to the undoing of sin's curse and the moral renewal of people's lives under God's grace. This lasting transformation stands as a permanent monument to the Lord's glory and faithfulness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the miraculous growth of trees as a permanent, literal physical renewal of the desert rather than merely a poetic picture of spiritual change.
